title: Preface
html:
Ask a group of engineers to design a new system and, before long, someone will walk to the whiteboard and start drawing boxes and arrows. An application programming interface (API) appears first, followed by a database, perhaps a cache, and a queue for processing requests later. Someone asks about traffic, another engineer asks who owns the data, and the diagram changes as the discussion continues. I have been in enough of these reviews to know how valuable that first drawing can be.

The drawing rarely settles what happens when a dependency becomes slow, or when two services record conflicting results for the same operation. A new feature can pass every test and still exhaust a resource that older features depend on. A request to another system can succeed on the far side just as the caller gives up waiting, whether that request books a seat, provisions a server, or transfers money. We need a way to decide what the user sees, what the application records, and how engineers recover without repeating an action that already happened. Those decisions belong in the design review as much as the database or queue on the whiteboard.

Baodium, a fictional online marketplace, gives us a running example throughout the book. Its product pages, orders, payments, and notifications give us operations we can follow from a line of code to the database and back to the customer. You will see why a feature flag did not protect a shared connection pool, what a payment timeout proves, why a replica may return an older value, and how delayed messages affect recovery. We will also use examples from software-as-a-service (SaaS) products, booking systems, social networks, continuous integration (CI) pipelines, and other applications. The marketplace is only the setting. The engineering principles apply to almost any system that serves users over a network.

The mathematics is introduced where it changes an engineering choice. We will spend more time on the transaction that prevents a duplicate action, the cache revision that prevents a stale decision, and the recovery procedure that has to run after a failed deployment. The examples use PostgreSQL, Redis, Kubernetes, Kafka, and other tools where their specific guarantees matter. Those details should be useful when you return to an application of your own.

As we progress, the design problems become less familiar. You will see how an engineer can establish an operation’s identity, decide which service owns a record, select the right communication mechanism, and revise a design after discovering that one of its guarantees does not survive a failure. Chapter 14 brings these decisions together in the review of Baodium’s European launch. Appendix B applies them to four other systems, including a change-validation service that must enforce policy revisions across deployment tools.

Each chapter contains a Decide for yourself case. I encourage you to consider the alternatives before reading why the team chose one. At the end, the Hidden Assumptions review records the evidence, limits, controls, and owners that would make the decision reviewable in production. Some chapters also examine a publicly documented incident, with the original source provided for further reading.

You do not need to have designed a distributed system before reading. Experience with a web application that serves requests over the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), a database, and a basic deployment process will be enough to follow the first examples. The numbers for Baodium are illustrative and are not performance benchmarks for the technologies we discuss. A production application needs measurements from its own environment. The security, privacy, and regulatory decisions also depend on the system being designed, so Appendix C includes a review of those requirements.

By the end, I hope you will be more comfortable starting with an unfamiliar problem, asking what the application must guarantee, and working from those guarantees toward a design that can be built, tested, operated, and improved. That is the kind of engineering judgment I have tried to develop through the examples in this book.

Adewale Obadimu
